label: meeting architecture
text: Results tools convert the GSD cycle into meeting routines and decision practices. One-to-ones, idea nurturing, staff meetings, debate meetings, and decision meetings each protect a different kind of work. Without meeting architecture, collaboration expands until it consumes execution time. Clear meeting types let managers preserve listening, debate, decision, and doing without mixing them into one crowded agenda.

label: Results discussion prompts
text: The official guide lists Results as Ch. 8 and asks about 1:1 meetings, nurturing new ideas, staff meetings, Big Debate, Big Decision, number of meetings, and meeting creep. Those items define the meeting architecture. Different meeting types should serve different collaboration jobs.

label: 1:1 meeting practice
text: The official guide ties Ch. 8 to Creating Effective 1:1 Meetings and Meet Like a Boss material. 1:1 meetings give direct reports a protected recurring channel rather than a manager-only status ritual. Regular individual meetings keep listening and guidance close to the work.

label: Meeting creep
text: The official guide names meeting creep as the risk that meetings take over time needed for execution. Meeting creep, execution time, staff meetings, and number of meetings anchor the results unit in calendar discipline. Collaboration must leave enough protected time for doing the work.

label: The official guide identifies Results as Ch. 8 in Part 2 Tools and Techniques.
text: The official guide identifies Results as Ch. 8 in Part 2 Tools and Techniques. Because Results follows the philosophy and team tools, it turns collaboration into operating routines. Treating results as pressure after relationship work. The unit designs how work gets done.

label: Ch. 8 asks managers how they approach 1:1 meetings.
text: Ch. 8 asks managers how they approach 1:1 meetings. Since 1:1s are recurring direct-report time, they should serve the employee's work and priorities. Using 1:1s only for manager status updates. That loses the protected listening channel.

label: Ch. 8 asks how managers nurture new ideas.
text: Ch. 8 asks how managers nurture new ideas. Because early ideas are fragile, they need a venue before full debate. Judging new ideas in the same meeting where decisions are made. Premature judgment can crush useful ideas.

label: Ch. 8 asks whether staff meetings match the recommended approach.
text: Ch. 8 asks whether staff meetings match the recommended approach. Since staff meetings can become catch-all rituals, managers need a clear purpose for them. Letting staff meetings absorb every collaboration need. A catch-all meeting blurs listening, debate, and decisions.

label: Ch. 8 names Big Debate meetings.
text: Ch. 8 names Big Debate meetings. Because debate tests ideas before commitment, separating it protects intellectual friction. Trying to decide before debate has done its work. The team may commit to an untested idea.

label: Ch. 8 names Big Decision meetings.
text: Ch. 8 names Big Decision meetings. Since decisions need closure, a separate decision forum prevents endless debate. Keeping debate open to avoid accountability. Without decision, execution cannot start.

label: Ch. 8 asks about the number of meetings suggested.
text: Ch. 8 asks about the number of meetings suggested. Because meeting load competes with work time, collaboration has to be designed economically. Assuming more meetings mean more alignment. Too many meetings can reduce execution.

label: Ch. 8 names meeting creep as a risk.
text: Ch. 8 names meeting creep as a risk. Since calendar expansion steals execution time, managers must remove or redesign meetings. Solving overload with another recurring meeting. That may deepen the execution bottleneck.

label: Results tools include impromptu feedback frequency alongside meeting design.
text: Results tools include impromptu feedback frequency alongside meeting design. Because feedback close to the work reduces review surprises, results improve before formal cycles. Waiting for formal reviews to guide performance. Late guidance cannot shape current execution.
